title: Administrative Distance: The Complete Beginner's Guide

scenes.narration: Two routing sources give you two different answers for the same place. Who does the router believe? The one with the best trust rating.

scenes.heading: The trusted messenger
scenes.narration: Imagine a boss getting reports from three people. A veteran vice president, a decent senior manager, and a brand new intern. When their reports disagree, the boss goes with the most trusted source. In networking, that trust score is called administrative distance. Lower means more trusted. And it's checked before the metric ever is.

scenes.heading: Distances to know
scenes.narration: Here are the numbers worth learning. Connected is zero. Static is one. Internal E I G R P is ninety. O S P F is one ten. R I P is one twenty. And external E I G R P is one seventy.

scenes.heading: Common mix-ups
scenes.narration: Three mix-ups. A lower metric does not beat a lower distance across protocols. Static routes can have a different distance if you set one. And external E I G R P is less trusted than O S P F.

items.right: AD is compared first, then metric

scenes.heading: Remember this
scenes.cta: Try the Courseiva administrative distance lab
scenes.narration: So, to recap. Administrative distance is how much the router trusts a source. Lower is better, and it beats the metric. Learn the big ones: zero, one, ninety, one ten, one twenty. Ready to practise? Try the Courseiva administrative distance lab.

points.t: AD = how much a source is trusted
